title: The Praying That Has to Happen Before the Preaching
subtitle: On sermon preparation as a spiritual act, why prayer in the study is not preliminary to exegesis but part of it, and how a praying preacher differs from a merely prepared one.

sections.title: The Thing We Skip First
sections.body:
When a week gets tight, prayer is the first thing to go. Tell the truth about that.

We will keep the exegesis. We will keep the commentaries open and the outline tight and the illustrations sharp. Those feel like the real work, because they produce something you can see by Saturday night. Prayer produces nothing you can point to. There is no page count for an hour on your face. So when Thursday arrives and the deadline is closer than the sermon, the praying is what we quietly cut, and we tell ourselves we will make it up later, and we never do.

This is not a scheduling problem. It is a doctrine problem. We have come to believe, in the marrow if not on paper, that the sermon is something we build and prayer is something we add. We have it backwards. The sermon is something God gives, and study is one of the means by which He gives it, and prayer is how we stay in the room where the giving happens. The preacher who studies without praying is a man laying bricks with no one to lift the wall.

sections.title: Prayer Is Part of the Exegesis
sections.body:
We talk as though there is study, and then there is prayer, as if they were two stations on a line. They are not.

The same Spirit who inspired the text is the Spirit you are asking to open it. The text is not a corpse you dissect with the right tools. It is a living word, and the One who breathed it is willing to be asked what He meant. This does not make the grammar optional. It does not let you skip the lexicon and call laziness faith. It means that the lexicon and the prayer belong to one act. You bend over the Greek and you say, open my eyes that I may see wondrous things out of your law, and you mean both halves at once.

The Reformers knew this and we have forgotten it. They held that the Word and the Spirit are not rivals but partners, that the Spirit works through the Word and not around it. So the praying preacher does not pray instead of studying or after studying. He prays while studying. He treats the desk as an altar. He asks the Author to be his teacher, and then he does the hard work of reading like a man who expects an answer.

sections.title: Pray the Text Into Yourself First
sections.body:
Before you ask what this text will do to your people, ask what it has done to you.

The oldest danger in our work is handling holy things until they stop being holy to you. You can study a passage about the fear of God and feel nothing. You can outline grace and remain hard. The way through is to refuse to move the text from your study to your sermon until it has first gone through your own chest. Take the passage and pray it back to God. If it convicts, let it convict you on Tuesday so you are not pretending on Sunday. If it comforts, receive the comfort before you offer it. Robert Murray McCheyne said the holiness of the minister is his people's greatest need, and there is no holiness manufactured in the pulpit that was not first received in the study.

This is slow and it cannot be faked. You will know you have done it when the sermon you carry to the room is not information you possess but a fire you barely contain. The people do not need a man who has read about the text. They need a man on whom the text has gone to work. Pray it into yourself, and you will not have to manufacture passion. You will have trouble hiding it.

sections.title: Pray for the People by Name
sections.body:
There is a kind of preaching that aims at no one and therefore hits no one. Prayer is the cure.

When you intercede for your congregation through the week, the sermon changes shape without your trying. You remember the widow in the third row when you reach the verse about comfort. You remember the man whose marriage is cracking when the text turns to forgiveness. You stop preaching to a crowd and start preaching to faces, and faces change how a man speaks. The general sermon, the one preached at a fog of anonymous people, comes from a study with no names in it. The piercing sermon comes from a study where you have been carrying real people to God all week.

So keep a list. Pray over the membership. Ask God to prepare the very hearts you will be addressing, because the same Spirit who is helping you write is already at work in the people who will hear. Spurgeon said he would rather pray than preach, and meant that the praying was the harder and the holier labor. The sermon is aimed in the prayer closet long before it is delivered from the platform. You are not only preparing a message. You are preparing a people, and you can only do that on your knees.

sections.title: The Difference Between Prepared and Prayed
sections.body:
Two preachers can stand up equally prepared and only one of them dangerous.

The difference is not eloquence and it is not learning. The prepared man delivers what he assembled. The prayed man delivers what he received, and there is a weight on it that no skill produces. You have sat under both. You know the difference even when you cannot name it. One man informs you. The other one finds you, and you walk out shaken, and you cannot quite say which sentence did it, because it was not a sentence. It was a Presence.

That Presence cannot be scheduled and it cannot be engineered, but it can be sought, and God has bound Himself to honor the seeking. So do not come to the pulpit having only studied. Come having begged. Come having wept over the text and over the people. Come empty enough to be filled.

The sermon is born in the study. But it is conceived on the knees.
